note: Ifera Hurmiz, mother of the Persian king Shapur, sent four hundred dinars to Rabbi Ami, who refused them. She sent them to Rava, who accepted them for the sake of peace with the kingdom. Rabbi Ami heard and was angry, citing a verse that the nations should not be helped to do good deeds. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Ami held the money should have gone to the gentile poor, that Rava had in fact given it to them, and that Rabbi Ami was angry only because he had not been told the end of the story.
why: The Gemara has been discussing a verse read as saying that the charity of other nations counts against them, while Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai held it atones for them. This story shows two Sages disagreeing over whether to take a gentile queen's charity.

people.name: Ifera Hurmiz
people.about: Mother of King Shapur; sends money for charity.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Refuses her gift and is angry that Rava accepts it.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Accepts the gift for the sake of peace with the kingdom.

terms.meaning: Keeping good relations with the ruling government, here the Persian crown.

note: A relative of Rav Idi bar Avin died and left a date tree. Another man took it, and each claimed to be the closer relative. In the end the man admitted that Rav Idi bar Avin was closer, and Rav Hisda gave him the tree. Rav Idi then asked to be repaid for the dates the man had eaten all along. Rav Hisda mocked him, asking whether this was the man called great: his claim rested on the other man's word, and until his admission that man had said he was closer.
why: The Gemara has been weighing when a person's own claim is believed. Here it notes that Abaye and Rava reject Rav Hisda's view: once the man admitted he was not the closer relative, he admitted he never had a right to the dates.

people.name: Rav Idi bar Avin
people.about: Claims a dead relative's date tree and its fruit.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The judge who gives Rav Idi the tree but refuses repayment for the fruit.

note: A firstborn son sold both his own share and his dead brother's share of their father's property before it was divided. His brother's orphaned sons went to eat dates from the field, and the buyers beat them. Their relatives protested that the buyers had bought the orphans' property and were now beating them too. The case came before Rava, who said the firstborn had done nothing: the sale was not valid.
why: Rav Pappa and Rav Pappi each quote Rava differently on whether a firstborn who takes an ordinary share gives up his extra portion. The Gemara says Rava never ruled on that directly; both views were inferred from this ruling.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who rules the firstborn's sale void.

terms.meaning: The eldest son, who inherits a double portion of his father's property.
A son who is not the firstborn and receives a single share.

note: Rav Zutra bar Toviyya's mother signed her property over to him because she wanted to marry Rav Zevid. She married him, and he divorced her. She came to Rav Beivai bar Abaye to get her property back. He ruled that she had given it so she could marry, and she had married, so the gift stood. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, mocked him for coming from a family of people cut off young, and argued that since she had said the gift was for the sake of the marriage, and she was now divorced, she could take it back.
why: The Gemara introduces a series of cases with a short memory aid, starting with this one. All of them concern gifts of property and whether the giver can take them back.

people.name: Rav Zutra bar Toviyya
people.about: The son who received his mother's property.

people.name: Rav Zevid
people.about: The man she married, who divorced her.

people.name: Rav Beivai bar Abaye
people.about: Rules that the gift to her son stands.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Mocks Rav Beivai and argues she can reclaim the property.

terms.meaning: When a woman about to marry writes her property over to someone else so that her husband does not gain rights to it.
An insult: Rav Beivai's family was said to descend from the priest Eli, whose descendants were cursed to die young.

note: In Bnei Brak a man sold some of the property he had inherited from his father, and then died. His family contested the sale, saying he had still been a minor when he died, so the sale was invalid. They asked Rabbi Akiva whether they could exhume him to examine the body. He said they were not permitted to disgrace him, and besides, the signs of puberty can change after death.
why: Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish disagree on how proof must be brought: by witnesses or by confirming the deed. Rabbi Yohanan cites this case against Reish Lakish, and the two argue over who held the property and who was contesting it.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Cites this case as an objection to Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
people.about: Also called Reish Lakish; the Sage being challenged.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Refuses to let the family exhume the dead man.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna.
Someone under the age of legal adulthood; a sale of inherited land by a minor is not valid.
Physical signs that showed a person had reached legal adulthood.

note: A man died owing money, leaving young orphans. His guarantor paid the creditor without first telling the orphans, and then wanted the orphans to repay him. Rav Pappa said that repaying a creditor is a religious duty, and minor orphans are not obligated in such duties. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, said that perhaps the father had already handed the creditor bundles of money before he died. By both views the orphans need not repay until they come of age.
why: The Gemara has been discussing guarantors and the rule that a creditor cannot collect from a debtor's property before claiming from the debtor. Afterward it asks when Rav Pappa's and Rav Huna's reasons would lead to different rulings.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Says minor orphans need not repay because they are not obligated in religious duties.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Says the father may already have repaid part or all of the debt.

terms.meaning: A person who promises to pay a loan if the borrower does not.
